Q: name '__file__' is not defined in jupyter notebook A:

The problem arise because of environment you are using. When you run python code in Jupyter notebook you are not running usual python environment - you are running it with iPython - interactive shell (version 7.12.0 is last currently). And it doesn't define hidden variable __file__ as mainstream python environment does - so it doesn't understand where to look for '/games' folder.

What you could do:

  1. Run it in usual python environment with __file__ variable defined
  2. Try placing your Jupyter notebook file in this project folder and using os.getcwd() instead of os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__)) or change path any other way that suits you.

Q: Prepend function call in other function in Python A:

There are a few different approaches to what you want to do, varying in "cleanliness" (as opposed to add-hoc hackish), easiness to do (and to understand and maintain later), dependency on Python implementation, and so on.

The limiting factor I see on which approach to use depends on how you can/want to interfere the declaration of the decorated function itself.

1. So, if you are in a position to change all the code that will make use of your decorator (or document it to others that will use it), the most straightforward, simpler, and which I think I would recommend, way to go, is to re-assign the function's default argument tuple (foo.func_defaults) at run time.

This approach requires that the variables you want to be overwritten in the running code be declared as function parameters with default values:

(I will use a simpler decorator than yours for documenting purposes)

new_args = (10,20)

def process(func):
    def new_func(*args, **kw):
        func_defaults = func.func_defaults
        func.func_defaults = new_args
        result = func(*args, **kw)
        func.func_defaults = func_defaults
        return result
    return new_func

@process
def foo(x=1, y =2):
    print x + y

And that "just works"(tm)

>>> foo()
30

2. Another approach, still requiring the decorated function to follow an specific pattern, is to declare all variables you want to be overwritten as global variables, and at call time, create a new function object, with everything just equal the original function, but changing its globals dictionary. Since you are creating a new function object for each call, this would be thread safe -0 however, you can't change variables that are declared as function parameters (as Python marks those as "local", and they can not be subsequently marked as "global")

from types import FunctionType

new_args = {"x":10, "y":20} 

def process(func):
    def new_func(*args, **kw):
        temp_func = FunctionType(func.func_code,
                                 new_args,
                                 func.func_name, 
                                 func.func_defaults,
                                 func.func_closure)
        return temp_func(*args, **kw)
    return new_func

        
@process
def foo():
    global x, y
    print x + y

3. Following the same approach, for each local variable that you want overridden, you'd list it at the top of the function as receiving a default value - like in

def foo(x=1,y=2):
   z= 3
   w = 4

And at run time you would re-build dynamically at each call, not just the function object, but its code object as well - you could call types.CodeType with the same parameters as the original func.func_code object, but for the "constants" parameter - which would replace the original's co_consts attributes.

I won't give an example for this way to do things, as it falls in the domain of "nice experimental hack, but horrendous for actual production code" - as it is too implementation dependent.

4. You can, on your decorator, set code tracing on - which is usually done by debugger utilities, so that you get a call back to a function you specify for each expression to be computed on the target code - You could them, enable the "settrace", and in your callback function fiddle with the local variables on the target function.
This is apparently simple, once you see the documentation for sys.gettrace - http://docs.python.org/library/sys.html#sys.settrace -- however it does have the small inconvenient of not working at all :-) This happens because although you do have right to read and write on the frame locals dictionary, Language optimizations not always fetch values from that dictionary when using them (if ever). So this straight forward example shows it not working:

>>> import sys
>>> def a():
...    b = 1
...    f = sys._getframe()
...    print f.f_locals
...    f.f_locals["b"] = 2
...    print b
... 
>>> a()
{'b': 1, 'f': <frame object at 0x1038cd0>}
1

5. Finally, you could do exactly as you say, and use Python's "dis" module and compiler functions to inject variable attribution inside your function code - directly on the bytecode. You'd have to: decompile the function's code object, successfully meddle with the bytecode to properly load your desired variables with the wanted values, recompile the byte code, recreate the code object (using the before mentioned types.CodeType call), passing an appropriate "constants" value to properly load your variables, recreate the function object from that and make your function call.

I will not enumerate the reasons why I find this approach less useful than others, neither try a reference implementation. It would work, if properly done, though, at least for cpython 2.x.

Q: Why do I need extra commands for printing documents? A:

Intro

From what I can understand, code that the person gave you is winGDI ( Graphics Device Interface ) commands. So instead of RAW commands sent directly to the printer, they are using the microsoft GDI format.

As you asked for a canonical answer, I will try to answer by providing references to official documentation (e.g. microsoft) when possible.

I see you have some of the information, already in your question... but without it the answer is not 100% complete.

What is GDI

Quoting wikipedia....

The Graphics Device Interface (GDI) is a legacy component of Microsoft Windows responsible for representing graphical objects and transmitting them to output devices such as monitors and printers. It was superseded by DirectDraw API and later Direct2D API. From: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_Device_Interface

Additionally, according to the article What are the differences between GDI, PCL and PostScript printers? ,

GDI transmits to output devices without needing to convert to a format such as PCL or Postscript. Most of the processing takes place in the OS.

About your code sample

You provided the following code:


if (::**StartDoc**(hDC, &docInfo) > 0)
    {
        if (::**StartPage**(hDC) > 0)
        {
            // Print the report
            ...
            ::**EndPage**(hDC);
        }
        else
        {
            sc = ::GetLastError();
        }
        ::EndDoc(hDC);

** These seem to be wingdi as they align fully with the microsoft documentation.**

So, for example:

The StartDoc function starts a print job. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-startdoca

The StartPage function prepares the printer driver to accept data. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-startpage

The EndPage function notifies the device that the application has finished writing to a page. This function is typically used to direct the device driver to advance to a new page. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-endpage

The EndDoc function ends a print job. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-enddoc

Your question/Issues

It's a little bit confusing - about what you are asking, but I will split it into 2 parts:

  1. Why do I need extra commands for printing documents? (As opposed to your customers)?
  2. On my PC, there is no way to make this work, so I asked for some assistance, and I got the advice to precede my code with the following lines of code:[...]but now I don't understand how the code was working previously on all those other systems.

Answer

It seems that your customers have printers that support non-GDI format. On the other hand, on your own system you need to pass the GDI commands in order to make it work. When you use GDI, windows converts the commands into commands that the printer can understand. These are probably graphics and test represented by raster image ( see: https://okiprinting-en-gb.custhelp.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/165/~/what-are-the-differences-between-gdi%2C-pcl-and-postscript-printers%3F ) .

Your customers probably have printers that support a RAW format like PostScript or PCL.

So there are atleast 2 ways of printing, raw (postscript, pcl) and gdi.

GDI vs PCL vs PS

I will be referencing the article from : What are the differences between GDI, PCL and PostScript printers?

We have already described GDI above, where most of the work is done by the OS and the driver.

PCL - Printer Command Language

Less features than GDI but the printer shares in the processing and the printing result is more consistent even across OS. It is apparently a printer standard, developed by HP since 1984 - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printer_Command_Language

For a list of commands, you can look at: https://www.pclviewer.com/resources/reference/#:~:text=Text%20Scale%20mode%20off,c%20(10U

PS - PostScript

PostScript (PS) is a page description language and dynamically typed, stack-based programming language. It is most commonly used in the electronic publishing and desktop publishing realm... https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PostScript

Here is an example from https://stackoverflow.com/a/46310437/1688441

%!PS
/Times-Bold findfont 36 scalefont setfont
72 684 moveto (Hello World!) show
showpage

So to summerize

Your customers are likely using printers (are they in publishing?) that natively understand PostScript or PCL. Then, your RAW data works directly there.

On your own system, your printer doesn’t support that language and you need Microsoft Windows GDI to translate it into something the printer can actually understand.

References

What are the differences between GDI, PCL and PostScript printers?

Graphic device Interface

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PostScript

Q: Notepad++ Multi editing A:

I use multi cursor editing since about 7 years and never use the shift + alt + arrow key for multi editing. All you need is a shortcut for the "multi select next", as demonstrated here:

Whenever a new cursor appeared in this amination, I pressed ctrl + d (or the shortcut you have configured for "multi select next"). See it explained in more detail https://npp-user-manual.org/docs/editing/ No mouse was used here and it is recoreded in real time.

This single shortcut covers most use cases for multiediting and also replaces "search & replace". When there is no repeating element to multiply your cursor, you can also select the newline character at the end of the line to multiply the cursor. Therefore, I recommend to learn only this single but very versatile shortcut.

Q: AUTH FAIL when calling Firebase function with Gemini AI/Embedding/Sentiment score A:

Firebase callable functions (and Firebase Authentication) aren't compatible with IAM authentication for Cloud Functions. GCP IAM is not in any way compatible with Firebase Auth - they represent different sets of user credentials with no overlap between them.

You need to set your function to allow public access (allUsers in GCP IAM terms) if you want to be able to invoke it from your mobile app. Then, if you want to restrict access to its functionality in some way based on the user's Firebase Authentication credentials, you need to write code in your function to check and enforce those restrictions.

See also:

  • Newly Created Firebase Functions Throwing UNAUTHENTICATED Error

  • Firebase onCall functions and Google Cloud Functions authentication showing call is unauthenticated

  • https://www.reddit.com/r/Firebase/comments/1nvu1ci/firebase_callable_function_unauthenticated/
